historic_survey.survey: Mission Dolores Neighborhood Historic Context Statement, adopted 2022
historic_survey.note: Listed as Mission Dolores among the properties in the survey area listed in or formally determined eligible for the National Register and the California Register, and as San Francisco Landmark No. 1. The statement gives the landmark's boundaries as covering both the mission of about 1781–1791 and the basilica of about 1918, spanning Assessor Block 3566, Lots 1 and 2; Planning names this lot the Mission San Francisco de Asís Cemetery and the roll classes it a vacant lot. The Department recommends the landmark designation report be amended, in consultation with community members, to cover the American Indian community — particularly the Ramaytush Ohlone — before, during and after the Mission era.

historical_record.description: The cornerstone of the permanent mission church was laid; the church, built by Indian neophytes to the missionaries' plan, was dedicated on 3 April 1791.
The church's interior decorations were whitewashed over and a white-painted wooden altar put up; the whitewash was later removed without much damage to the decoration.
A large brick church was dedicated just north of the mission church; it was so badly damaged in the 1906 earthquake that it was razed, while the old church showed no damage.
The grading of Dolores Street was ordered, which added brick underpinning and a flight of entrance steps to the church facade and set back the cemetery walls.

A restoration directed by the architect Willis Polk inserted a steel frame of seven trusses on columns set into the adobe walls from outside, without disturbing the original adobe, ceiling or roof trusses; the original roof tiles were relaid, made up with tiles from Mission San Antonio de Padua.
The reinforced-concrete parish church begun in 1913 north of the adobe mission, in place of the 1876 brick church wrecked in 1906, was completed; Pope Pius XII made it a minor basilica in 1952.

Part of the mission cemetery along 16th Street was removed when the street was extended to Church Street; more went in 1901 for the grading of Dolores Street, and to new buildings in 1932, 1953 and 1955. Of up to 10,000 people buried there, about 5,000 of them Indian neophytes, some 200 headstones remain.

A wooden headstone honoring two Ohlone neophytes buried in unmarked graves in 1804 and 1807 was added to the cemetery, beside a traditional tule reed house built the same year to commemorate the Native Californians who built and ran the mission.
